qs.q: During an evaluation of mucosal immunology in a patient with HIV, the role of helper T cell subsets in maintaining the intestinal barrier is examined. What is a primary role of Th17 cells in maintaining intestinal homeostasis?
o: They directly inhibit the production of defensins and mucin to save energy
They promote direct bacterial translocation across the gut barrier
They induce the expression of claudins which are tight junction components
They stimulate massive viral replication and rapid mucosal fibrosis
qs.e: Th17 cells are involved in intestinal homeostasis and epithelial regeneration, and they induce the expression of claudins which form epithelial tight junctions. They stimulate, rather than inhibit, defensins and mucin.

qs.q: An immunology research fellow is reviewing the pathogenesis of SLE. Which immunologic abnormality is directly mentioned in the notes?
o: Hypoactivity of B and T lymphocytes
qs.e: The notes explicitly state that SLE features the overproduction of IL-6 and IL-10, alongside B and T lymphocyte hyperactivity. Furthermore, apoptosis is increased rather than decreased, and immune complex clearance is impaired.

qs.q: An immunology panel returns for a patient being evaluated for systemic lupus erythematosus, showing positive anti-Smith antibodies. Which of the following best characterizes this autoantibody?
o: It correlates closely with central nervous system involvement.
It is present in a minority of patients and has stable titers.
It fluctuates rapidly with changes in daily corticosteroid doses.
It is present in nearly all patients with renal disease flares.
qs.e: Anti-Smith antibodies are found in 25-30% of SLE cases with high specificity, but unlike anti-dsDNA, their titer does not fluctuate with disease activity. They remain relatively stable over time despite clinical changes.

qs.q: During tumour immunology surveillance, which host immune cells are specifically responsible for recognising and killing tumour cells that lack MHC class I expression as an immune evasion mechanism?
qs.e: Natural killer (NK) cells eliminate tumour cells that downregulate or lack MHC I expression to evade cytotoxic T cells. Cytotoxic T lymphocytes require MHC I presentation to recognise their targets.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Immunology is the study of the body’s defence system and its disorders. In low‑resource hospitals, recognising infections, immune deficiencies and inflammatory syndromes is vital for rapid, lifesaving care.

b: Adaptive immunity: B‑cell antibodies, T‑cell responses
sections.p: The immune system protects against pathogens and regulates inflammation. In East Africa, infections such as HIV, TB, malaria and schistosomiasis, plus endemic autoimmune and allergic conditions, shape clinical presentations.

b: Adaptive defects: antibody deficiency, T‑cell deficiency
sections.p: Immune responses are divided into innate and adaptive arms. Defects can be inherited or acquired. Clinical clues include pattern of infection, timing, and laboratory markers.

t.b: Assess neutrophil count – neutropenia suggests innate defect or HIV
Low IgG indicates antibody deficiency; normal IgG with recurrent infections suggests T‑cell problem

Detects Plasmodium antigens; guides antimalarial therapy

sections.p: Patients often present with atypical infections, severe disease, or paradoxical reactions. Early recognition of immune status directs empiric therapy, infection control and referral.

Detects TB cavities or bacterial pneumonia
